Network security protocols prevent unauthorized access through authentication mechanisms, encryption standards, access control lists, and intrusion detection systems that monitor and filter network traffic. These layered defenses protect against eavesdropping, man-in-the-middle attacks, and unauthorized network penetration.

Malware analysis tools help identify malicious behavior patterns, network communications, persistence mechanisms, and evasion techniques employed by sophisticated threats. Sandboxes, debuggers, and disassemblers provide controlled environments for examining malware functionality without compromising production systems.

System hardening techniques include removing unnecessary services, applying security patches, configuring access controls, enabling logging mechanisms, and implementing defense-in-depth strategies to reduce attack surface and improve security posture against various threat vectors.

Public key cryptography uses a mathematically linked key pair: a public key that anyone may use to encrypt or verify, and a private key kept secret for decryption or signing. Its security rests on problems such as integer factorisation or discrete logarithms being computationally hard.

Hash functions map arbitrary input to a fixed-length digest and are designed to be preimage and collision resistant. They underpin password storage, integrity checking, and digital signatures, and are typically combined with salts when protecting stored credentials.

The TCP three-way handshake establishes a reliable connection. The client sends a SYN segment, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client confirms with an ACK, after which sequence numbers track ordered, acknowledged delivery of the byte stream.

The domain name system resolves human-readable names into IP addresses through a hierarchy of root, top-level, and authoritative servers. DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures so resolvers can verify that responses have not been tampered with in transit.

Operating systems isolate processes using virtual memory, privilege rings, and access control checks in the kernel. Each process sees its own address space, and transitions to privileged mode occur only through well-defined system call interfaces.

Secure software development integrates security throughout the lifecycle: threat modelling during design, static and dynamic analysis during implementation, dependency scanning in continuous integration, and coordinated disclosure processes after release.

Version control systems track changes to source code over time, allowing developers to branch, merge, and review modifications. Commit histories provide an audit trail that is valuable both for debugging regressions and for investigating security incidents.

Firewalls enforce a network security policy by inspecting traffic against a rule set. Stateless filters examine individual packets, stateful firewalls track connection state, and application-layer gateways interpret protocol semantics before forwarding.

Transport Layer Security protects data in transit by negotiating cipher suites, authenticating servers with certificates issued by trusted authorities, and deriving ephemeral session keys that provide forward secrecy for the encrypted channel.

Identity and access management assigns permissions according to the principle of least privilege. Role-based and attribute-based models, combined with multi-factor authentication and periodic access reviews, limit the impact of any single compromised account.

Relational databases organise data into tables with defined schemas and enforce integrity through primary keys, foreign keys, and constraints. Parameterised queries separate code from data and are the standard defence against injection flaws.

Logging and monitoring provide visibility into system behaviour. Centralised collection, structured formats, time synchronisation, and tamper-resistant storage make logs useful for both operational troubleshooting and forensic reconstruction.

Data structures such as arrays, linked lists, hash tables, and balanced trees offer different trade-offs between lookup, insertion, and deletion cost. Choosing appropriately is central to writing efficient and predictable programs.

Backups protect against data loss from hardware failure, human error, or ransomware. A common guideline keeps three copies on two media types with one offsite, and recovery is only trustworthy once restores have been tested.

Virtualisation and containerisation package workloads with their dependencies. Hypervisors provide strong hardware-level isolation, while containers share a kernel and rely on namespaces and control groups for lighter-weight separation.

Penetration testing is an authorised assessment in which testers probe systems for weaknesses under an agreed scope and rules of engagement. Findings are documented with severity ratings and remediation guidance for the system owners.

Incident response follows a structured cycle of preparation, detection, containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons learned. Clear runbooks and communication plans shorten the time between detection and restoration of normal service.
